chapters.title: remember us, remember that we loved
chapters.html:
Strange how hunger can be felt in the bones.

At some point, after acids consume the flesh, the pain in the stomach subsides. The organism converts to cannibalism, body feeding off itself, leaving behind a pestilent gaping hole that keeps on growing by gnawing and eating and chewing the peripheral organs. It stops hurting once it has devoured everything, like a satiated beast, a scavenger. Only the bones remain, aching and brittle.

Mydei's body has always been his worst enemy. Unkillable, unlovable.

It has been drifting in the shallow waters of the Sea of Souls for around two months, cold water licking at the bones sticking out of its emaciated shell.

Mydei's mind has long since left somewhere else, drowning in a no less familiar sea—the sea of his memories.

The last thing he remembers is a hard and humid boat deck, tailbone digging into the wooden boards as a stranger's hands dropped him unceremoniously on them. Freshly fished out of the water, Mydei stared at the men before him with bulging eyes.

The voyagers eyed him in return, faces turning uneasy at the skeletal creature they had caught in their net. It was far from being a common occurrence to come across a living person in ghosts' territory—Mydei was well aware of that fact. He would even argue that it was bad omen. At least, that was what other humans before them had considered him to be.

"Are you alright?" A voice asked him, and Mydei looked up at the body that was attached to those hands, the ones that had dug him out of the endless sea.

The man had soft features, his eyes held a gentleness that was wholly unfamiliar to Mydei, and his brows were furrowed in concern. Mydei observed with rapt attention the way his long brown hair swayed with the wind, the way creases formed on his forehead and the corner of his mouth stretched into a thin line at Mydei's unresponsiveness.

"Nikador, what I am saying! Of course you're not, look at you," the same man pitied him. He turned towards his companions. "Do we still have some food left? Even just a chunk of bread–"

Before he could finish and become Mydei's salvation, another man, older in appearance and wearing a white and red priest robe, grabbed him by the arm.

"Don't," he said, tone shaky. He looked ghastly and his eyes were riveted on Mydei, as if Mydei would pounce on them like some untamed animal if they dared to look away.

The younger man sent a curious look to his companion, then to Mydei slumped against the boat mast like a dead man. "What do you mean?" He hissed when the grip on his arm strengthened.

"Throw him back in," the priest ordered. "Look at his armband. His tattoos."

The young man's gaze raked down Mydei's malnourished body, followed the bold red patterns inked on it, and landed on the golden armband that had slipped off his bicep and now circled his bony wrist.

Mydei watched as terror disfigured the young man's face. He could not detach his regard from him as he heard him pronounce his next words in a breath, "i-it's the cursed crown prince."

Any ounce of concern had vanished in the tensed atmosphere.

Had he been more skin than bone at that moment, Mydei would have bared his teeth and lived up to that fallacious title. Growled to prevent those fanatics of his father's reign from getting their hands on him, before diving back in the waters like a king returning home. But his body, heavy with weariness, could no longer fight; his claws were clipped, his fangs were dull.

The same hands that prayed to Nikador and revered Eurypon seized him roughly, lifted him as easy as a child, and tossed him into the sea. Mydei watched their faces blur along the waves above before he could commit to memory the details of them, heard the sighs of relief wheezing out of their lungs while his were filling up with water.

Back when his cheeks were rounder and his rugged clothes hung loosely around his frame, they used to pity him for far longer—enough time for Mydei to stuff his mouth with bread and steal from their rations what his small hands could manage to grab. He used to mock these adults, terrified of a child who could not yet reach an altar but blessed by the divine, all due to a mad man's orders and a few priests' deceits.

As he slowly sinks into the sea, he thinks of Gorgo, his mother. Strong and loving Gorgo, whose warm embrace protected him through twelve springs. Until her arms fell loudly to the ground and he was the one holding up her limp body.

He thinks of companions he does not recognise, fighting alongside him, defending his honour. Of a man, standing tall, blue cape floating in the wind and broad sword in one hand, guarding his back and glancing at him with a smile on his face.

Mydei realises that his brain is dying, conjuring idyllic images to make his death seems more gentle in one last effort, for no one would ever gaze at him with such tenderness in their eyes.

So he thinks of Eurypon, glaring down at him with frigid eyes, and he imagines that, unlike his mother's, his father's embrace must feel as cold as the waters hugging him right now, pulling him down to meet Death.

—

When Mydei regains consciousness, he is laying on the firm dry ground and cobbles dig into thick, full, and defined, back muscles. Even though his body mass is denser, he feels lighter, relieved that his body has been reset to its default state; a natural musculature built on years of swimming and fighting against the tide endlessly.

He must have died again.

He does not dwell on it for too long as it is all too familiar. With time, he even learned to be grateful to Death. It grants him a new functional body, the perfect tool to fend off sea monsters and drag himself to the next shore. It also satiates his hunger, like forcibly feeding him the souls of those who have drowned before him.

There's a heat source near him. Mydei turns onto his sides to allow the flames to lick at his cheeks, revelling in their warmth. Eyes still closed, he lets out a content sigh; fire always provided him a comfort the waters cannot give. His mind supplies him with images of campfires with loyal friends whom he cannot assign any names. He blinks his eyes open.

From the moment Mydei regained consciousness, he knew he was not alone, having sensed a presence watching over him from across the fire.

The presence tries to lay low but Mydei can feel its sheer power vibrating in his own bones. The wind bends around it like a great obstacle, a force out of this world that even nature carefully avoids. It is waiting, placid, and Mydei wonders if this honourable opponent isn't simply giving him ample time to emerge from his deathly slumber.

He stares at the strange figure clad in black through the dancing flames.

"Are you Death?" He asks, and the shadow flinches. A human-like reaction.

It laughs but it sounds hollow. "You could say that." At Mydei's lack of laughter, the man quickly adds, "but, no. I am … human." He hesitates on the last word.

Mydei hums and wriggles closer to the fire, savouring a last moment of peace. "That's what they used to say too. Before pulling me down to the bottom of the sea with them," he says.

"How old would you be now?"

Mydei's eyebrows shoot up, not expecting such a question from a stranger. He prompts himself up on his arms and eyes the man distrustfully, but struggles to see anything other than darkness wrapping around his broad frame. With the hood obscuring his face, Mydei can only make out a glimpse of his chin.

"Who are you?"

The man sighs quietly and takes a moment to reply.

"You can call me Khaslana."

"Khaslana," Mydei repeats and he frowns at the name; it is unfamiliar, yet the name rolls easily on his tongue. He answers regardless of the suspiciousness of the situation. "I should be twenty by now. Hard to tell when your metric system is based on your deaths."

Khaslana inhales sharply and his fists tightens around the fabrics of his tattered trousers.

"I'm sorry." His voice is shaky on the edges and the apology sounds genuine. Mydei's frown deepens, sceptic.

"I should have come sooner, Mydeimos."

In a fraction of seconds the stranger's back hits hard the cobblestones covering the shore. He makes no sound of pain, hands coming to grab weakly, almost gently, at the claws squeezing around his neck. His hood is still concealing half of his face and, from atop him, Mydei can see his mouth form a tight line and his teeth dig into the plump of his lips.

Mydei sits on his waist, heavy, expression wild. "Who sent you?" He barks.

The man's hands slide to Mydei's wrists, try to allow some air to flow through his trachea. He makes a few choked sounds but manages to croak. "I-I'm no a-ally of your … father."

"Why should I believe you? How do you–"

Mydei shakes him closer and the hood finally slips to reveal the stranger's visage. Mydei freezes in place.

The man's skin is pale, with a grey-ish undertone that makes Mydei question if he is made of clay rather than flesh, and there are small cracks, almost imperceptible, scattered all over his face; splitting on his temples, coursing along the sharp edges of his prominent cheekbones.

Yet, he looks beautiful.

White short hair frames his face and Mydei feels the itch to reach out and run his hands through it, to trace the scars adorning his skin almost in awe. Khaslana's features are no doubt handsome, and what strikes the most about his appearance is those two blue orbs ornamented with gold boring through Mydei. The emotion swimming in them is utterly foreign to Mydei but he is physically unable to look away.

He stares and stares at Khaslana, drowning deeper in his eyes than he ever did in the Sea of Souls. He does not even react when Khaslana caresses his wrists away, lips stretching into a subdued smile. The touch is electric, familiar, and a sudden headache overcomes Mydei, prompting him to entirely let go. He grabs at his own head and groans in pain.

Khaslana's eyes grow worried and he sits up urgently. Mydei's rear glides against the rough fabrics of his cloak to land on his lap. "Are you alright?" He asks, worried.

It only serves to worsen Mydei's headache and a rush of fuzzy memories mix with the confusion. His visions blurs, his heartbeat increases, his grip at his hair tighten, painfully so, and blurry images surge in his mind one after another. The pain hinders Mydei's ability to register any of them; as if flipping through a picture book, he watches them pass before his eyes for barely a second, panting heavily.

Khaslana stays silent, and it takes a moment for Mydei to still his breath. Soon the pain evaporates, leaving behind a faint dull sound and a lot of questions. He sees in his field of vision Khaslana's gloved hand approaching his face and he moves it away before his touch can land on his forehead.

"… I'm alright." His voice is rougher than Khaslana's now. "Just hungry."

Khaslana does not question him further, though there is a knowing glint in those sharp eyes of his, and he smiles up at him, gently. Again. "I made some food," he says and tilts his head in the direction of the fire.

Mydei glances at it and sees two roasted and juicy tentacles on a stick. Sea monsters. "I'm not hungry," he curtly replies.

"You still keep up those princely manners of yours no matter what," Khaslana laughs. It sounds lively.

The melodious sound wraps around Mydei's heart but he chooses to ignore it. He ignores the tug at his heart as well, ignores the implications of Khaslana's claims. Ignores the familiarity of it all, the memories that make no sense, like dispersed puzzle pieces that can not fit together yet.

He, however, can not ignore any longer their bodies flushed together with the way Khaslana's hand has claimed his thigh. It spreads a fire in his stomach hotter than the one currently burning their food. A blush creeps up Mydei's nape and he quickly gets off Khaslana's lap to sit beside him, mindful to put some distance between them.

Khaslana does not appear as affected as him; he readjusts his position to properly face the fire after dusting off his black garment—even though the thing is clearly already tattered and sandy from years of battle—features scarily neutral again.

Mydei observes the flames trying to reach for the sky while keeping a keen eye on the man sitting beside him. He sighs inwardly and decides to tune out his instinct screaming at him to flee, to run away from the obvious danger sitting beside him. Disguised in an magnetic envelop that Mydei can not seem to pull away from, hidden behind a sweet smile.

The island Khaslana took him to is small, so running away would mean returning to the sea. Though he has regained a functional body, Mydei is not eager to test its limits again; he has repeated that experience for around a decade and that was enough to deter him from doing so tonight.

A silent stretches between them which helps to lull the storm of feelings and visions raging inside him. Khaslana fiddles idly with the sticks planted on the ground, turning them around to cook the non-charred parts of their food, and Mydei reads some awkwardness in his movements. Not that unaffected in the end, huh.

"So, who sent you?" Mydei interrupts him.

Khaslana pauses and his expression turns conflicted. "Myself," he replies.

Mydei side-eyes him, not quite understanding what he means, but Khaslana's gaze no longer meets his.

Mydei takes the occasion to observe him. The slope of his nose, the unruly hair on top of his head, the enticing golden sun tattoo peeking out from his collar, his muscular build that looks a tad bigger than Mydei remembers—does he remember?

"Has no one truly come for you all these years?" Khaslana asks after a beat.

Mydei's eyes goes back to his face. He scoffs. "And who would have come for me?"

"Krateros."

"You mean the man who chose to stay by Eurypon's sides even after witnessing that mad king pierce through my mother's back while she was protecting me?"

Khaslana's mouth opens and closes immediately. He averts his gaze from the fire, eyes scanning over Mydei's impassive face instead.

His mother's death is one of the rare wounds his body has not yet managed to erase; it remains as a deep cut over his heart, a never-closing gash, for nothing could appease the grief of losing the person who loved you the most. But Mydei learned at a young age that crying was a useless thing and would not bring her back. His tears only served to expand the Sea of Souls that took her.

"And your companions? They were your friends."

"Friends?" Mydei's voice goes higher, dumbfounded. "I was kept in a room for years after he discovered that no death of mine was foreseen by the oracles in his kingdom. I have no friend, nor companion."

Khaslana takes the information in and Mydei can practically see the cogs in his head working, lining up events that are unfamiliar to him.

Khaslana sighs. "I see." He does not inquire more.

Instead, he casts his gaze downwards to the tentacles slowly decaying, smearing black onto the stones. The stench irritates Mydei's nose, makes him want to vomit, and Khaslana throws the twigs away as neither of them want or need to eat.

And you, why did you come for me?

The question burns on the tip of Mydei's tongue but he keeps it there, lets it linger for longer. His shoulders tense up and he feels an acute ache in his back, low on his spine; his body seems to know the answer, his bones remember something he can not yet.

"And you, where are your companions?" It's his turn to ask questions so he goes with the safest option.

Khaslana stares at him, pensive. He does that a lot, Mydei notices; thinking, choosing his words carefully. Yet, his thoughts are loud to Mydei, like a book he has already read before.

"I fear I've long been ahead of them. Now, it's only me," he says. There's regret and longing slipping from his words.

"Can't you walk the same pace as them?"

Khaslana's brows arch on his forehead before pressing together. "It's not that easy, you don't know how many times I've tried." His shoulders sag and he runs a hand through his hair, obvious signs of pent-up frustration leaking from the cracks on his face. "It just gets … tiring."

Mydei hums in response.

There is clearly a heavy burden, the size of the world, on Khaslana's back. One that makes him hunch over that fire, one that slowly buries the man he used to be under its crushing weight. The tale of a heroic man comes to Mydei's mind.

A man whose fate was greater than the sky above Amphoreus, yet no living souls acclaimed the exploits of on his way back home. What welcomed the hero was blood, splattered on walls, oozing from bodies, thick gold blending with dark red.

Had Mydei read an epic like that before? Leather-bound book bigger than his thighs spread out on his lap, small fingers leafing through, and innocent eyes glinting at the hero's perseverance and valour?

He believes his mother could have read it to him after much arguing about it not being appropriate for a child. Little Mydei loved those stories after all. He would smile up at her with crooked teeth, beg her to continue just for more time with her. At night, he would dream of a successful end for the hero.

Mydei does not know where those memories are being unearthed from—assuming they are even real—but Khaslana fits the Deliverer in his mind like a glove, similar to those metallic ones he wears; rusted with a tinge of red on the edges. Mydei thinks those would suit him as well, to tear monsters apart with ease. Though he has always preferred gold to silver.

The puzzle pieces are assembling. Mydei's head feels clearer. Despite still being unable to visualise the whole picture, he answers sincerely, "as long as you're doing what you believe to be right."

Khaslana stiffens for a second. Mydei almost finds it too easy to read into a man who is supposed to be a stranger in this lifetime.

"You never change, Mydei," Khaslana mourns but his smile remains soft. Its effect is disarming.

Mydei scoots closer to him, seeking the warmth radiating from Khaslana rather than the heat of the unattended fire gradually dying down. He bumps their knees together.

"Tell me about myself then. What I'm like in your memory."

Khaslana's eyes widen and something achingly fragile flashing in them. Mydei sees the moment realisation dawns on him, hears the sound of his heart picking up.

"You … you remember. How?"

There is hope—expectations—in his voice, and Mydei feels bad for shattering them. "I don't know. Not everything," he explains. "But it's like my soul knows yours. Recognises you."

Khaslana's lips tremble. His sharp nails scratch the surface of the cobbles below, sending them rolling under his palms, and he takes a deep breath. It only hits Mydei now how the expression he has worn since that hood slipped to unveil his deep blue eyes was one of a lover reuniting with his beloved. It squeezes Mydei's heart painfully.

He looks at Khaslana and he bleeds affection, as if this pure feeling had been inside him all along, stored in that repulsive body of his. Among the ugly hatred and the desire for vengeance.

Longing fills Khaslana's gaze just the same, yet his smile falters slightly, the corners turning down. He seems upset. "I thought for a second we could finally–" He falls into silent and shakes his head. "Forget it."

The words prick at Mydei but he says nothing, only lowers his gaze to the moon encrusted over Khaslana's chest. He wants to reach out and trace its cutting edges. But, even though their shoulders are almost brushing, Khaslana is far away, standing in the darkest parts of Mydei's memory. Perhaps, he reckons, it is cruel of him to give this man hope when all Mydei has are blurry images and dormant feelings cautiously awakening to the deep timber of Khaslana's voice.

Before he can apologise or defer the conversation, Khaslana breaks the heavy silent.

"You stayed true to yourself and kept your principles close to your heart till every end you met. You fought for what you believed in—for your people, for Amphoreus. And for us." He chuckles ruefully. "And fight, you did. So stubborn and defiant."

He pauses, reminiscing on the past for the both of them. A smile is back on his lips.

"But that's how we get to know each other. We learn to anticipate our opponent's movements until our thoughts, our breath, our bodies, become one and the same."

Mydei recalls the feelings of taut muscles rolling under his fingertips and large calloused hands on him and he blushes furiously. Khaslana continues.

"I don't think anyone understands me more than you. I guess that explains why you always stand on my path. To make sure I never stray from it."

He holds Mydei's stare with such sincerity that the blond uncharacteristically turns his head away, praying that his fiery mane is enough to hide his reddening ears.

"This is uncomfortable," he mutters, and Khaslana laughs, loud and heartily. It reverberates against the walls of Mydei's torso and its echoes shape the figure of the man inside his mind. Though his hair is a different shade and his skin is painted a pretty pale rose, his features takes after Khaslana's.

Mydei's head pulses again but he does not stir, does not try to rub the ache away. He allows the memories to flow in—a chaotic torrent, increasing in its violence. Unlike the Sea of Souls, he readily dives in it.

"Tell me about–" you. Us. He does not know which one to pick.

He only wishes for this moment between them to last longer. Parts of their shared past are still clouded by dark grey masses akin to the ones in the sky above them, and Mydei knows they do not have long before it comes down to that part of their story.

Khaslana nods. He does not need Mydei to finish.

"We fight a lot at first—sword clashing with fists and words tearing walls down. Fights turn into spars and daily rendezvous on the rooftops of Okhema, games of chase that feel … liberating. I think we both enjoy it equally. I'm not sure about everyone else though."

"There are days where we cause quite the ruckus. Like this one time I swiped you off your feet and you sent a tile flying by slipping on it. Poor Theodoros got the scare of his life! I had planned to buy that pot we broke, you know. Even if you called it an affront to the arts," he giggles. Mydei does not know. Still, he listens attentively.

He can visualise it now, a sea of colourful roofs in a city gleaming under a blinding light that no cloud can bedim. Below his feet, layers of mismatched drapery cover the streets. The streets are busy, a crowd forms around every stand. The smell of food, leather, and ash, blend into the air.

Across from him on another rooftop, Khaslana is there, perfectly poised. In his hand is a wooden sword that taps rhythmically against his palm, and on his lips is a smirk, taunting Mydei.

Mydei wants to mock the tiny weapon. Ridiculous, he'd scoff. Wounds are temporary on his body and scars fade as easily as rubbing off ink with a wet rag. Yet, the sight of that sword warms his heart and he feels the corners of his mouth lift, matching Khaslana's smirk.

He shifts closer to the present Khaslana. Their shoulders touch, their thighs brush, and Khaslana unconsciously relaxes against him.

"Aglaea did not appreciate it either. But it was fun to see you with your tail tucked between your legs in front of her."

"What else do we do?" Mydei encourages him to continue. Khaslana gladly do so, filling up the gaps in Mydei's mind.

"We lay on those same rooftops at night—though night never falls. Often you stay quiet, in a place of your own. You close your eyes and your chest rises and falls evenly, leaving me to wonder what the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos is dreaming about during his rare moments of peace. When I try to leave you to rest, you always catch my wrist."

Mydei remembers the safety of arms around him. Confidence, secrets formerly locked away, whispered for each other's ears only while the city is dormant. Doubts fading with just one touch. One shared smile. One kiss.

Something seizes him at the throat.

Images are overflowing in his brain and he can not stop the burst of feelings that follows, exploding below his ribcage in ripples. It spreads to his fingertips and Mydei itches to reach out to the man by his side, who is still talking about poems and libraries and things Mydei already knows—already lived.

These feelings he recognises them. Remembers them. They have a name, carved into his bones, seared onto his soul.

"—Phainon?"

Mydei's thumb traces the underside of a pale and a hollow cheek, and blue eyes dart frantically all over his face, taking on a colour deeper than the sea a few meters ahead of them. Only the sound of the waves sweeping the shore fill the silent around them. Water wells in Phainon's eyes yet tears don't fall from them since the Deliverer has long forgotten how to cry.

Phainon's head drops to Mydei's shoulder, nose and hair tickling the side of his neck as he inhales deeply, tries to settle his breathing. It is broken sob when he speaks. "Mydei."

Mydei's guts twist hard and it feels suffocating. He can feel Phainon's mouth part against his collarbone as Phainon struggles to say more than Mydei's name.

Mydei's hand comes up to lay on top of Phainon's head and it tangles with white hair strands like it has done so many times before. He brings his face closer to Phainon's.

Close, he can smell the unmistakable scent of blood and death and destruction clinging to his cloak. Lingering underneath the deathly fragrance, is the scent of wheat, bread and the sun. Unmistakably Phainon's. Mydei nuzzles his hair.

"Do what you came here to do," he orders, but his command is no louder than the wind swaying the dying flames.

Phainon tenses in his arms. His hands clutches tightly at Mydei's tunic. "Duel me," he says, voice low.

A small smile forms on Mydei's lips and he closes his eyes—presses Phainon against him and lets the emotions of thousands of lifetimes course through his veins. He feels and he feels, and his smile stretches.

A hand circles his waist to rest flat on his lower back. "Duel me, like you've always done," Phainon begs. At Mydei's unresponsiveness, he persists. "Ask me to duel you." His hold on Mydei is bruising. Familiar with the pain, Mydei accepts it.

He cradles Phainon's face in his hands, feels how tense his jaw is and sees how wan is expression has turned. He brushes a few strands of hair away to leave a kiss on his forehead.

"It gets tiring, doesn't it?" Mydei mouths against the cold skin. Phainon's lips bob once. Twice. And then, he nods.

And it is tiring—so tiring. A weariness that makes them bend forwards, that nestles in their bodies and hinders their steps. And yet, they walk. They fight, and they kill, and they die. Again and again.

Each cycle adds an extra weight on Phainon's back and he carries it to the next one, marching down a different path from the companions he swore to protect. Their memories vanish and only he remains, aside, fated to watch them burn themselves chasing after an artificial dream—a promised era that never comes as long as he stands against fate. Against them.

A hand leaves Mydei's hip. Then, a rustling sound followed by metals knocking against each other ring in Mydei's ear. He embraces Phainon close.

"Why won't you fight?" Phainon asks, distraught. His hand on Mydei's back slides further up tattooed skin, finding its way to that familiar spot. "It… it isn't like you to surrender."

Mydei chuckles. "This isn't surrender," he says as he tucks a stray strand of hair behind Phainon's ear. His expression is terribly tender and Phainon's gaze can not tear away from it, pupils growing wider, imprinting every detail of Mydei into his brain. "It's acknowledgement."

He leans slightly backwards, digging Phainon's fingers deeper into his spine. "Besides, this is proof enough of your determination."

No apology, no justification, had spilled from Phainon's mouth since they had reunited—it would have been the last thing Mydei had wanted to hear. Neither of them knew if the route he had taken was the right one, but it was the one Phainon had chosen and Mydei trusted his judgment.

Phainon's intentions to search for him in this cycle had never been about rescuing him—those were pretty clear the moment Mydei had glimpsed at that ominous figure from across the fire. And it was a such a relief to Mydei that these intentions had not changed, even with his memories back. Even as they held each other tight and their hearts beat in unison.

The cold metal of a blade traces around Mydei's waist and up his back, stopping right above his weakness, and Mydei smiles, content. He kisses Phainon gently, slowly, and breathes against his lips, "I believe in you, Deliverer."

The tip of the blade is already piercing at Mydei's skin and Phainon squeezes his eyes shut, bracing himself. Wet and hot liquids dribble along Mydei's spine and on Phainon's cheeks as he kisses him again.

"Please, remember us in the next cycle," Phainon implores, voice rendered to a broken whisper. He plunges the knife to the hilt in one smooth motion. Mydei's face distorts on instinct and he hisses quietly against his lips.

Golden blood stains silver gloves, and Phainon presses one last kiss on his lips before a dizziness overcomes Mydei, his head dropping onto Phainon's shoulder, who caresses his back in what he hopes is a soothing manner.

"Remember that I've loved you in every lifetime," Phainon says, and Mydei wants to answer that he does; deep within himself, his heart had remembered. But his tongue is now heavy in his mouth, his muscles are unresponsive and his body is limp like the corpses that litter below the waters encircling them.

In his last moments, he is glad his back is to the Sea of Souls and the last thing he can see, smell and feel, is Phainon. He knows the Sea can no longer reach him in his arms. Countless times had he imagined how Death would take him if It was given the right.

He had not imagined that Death would be a lover.
